core.p: Many familiar effects are explained by objects tending to keep their state of motion.
bullets: **Tablecloth trick**: pulled quickly, the cloth moves but the plates, with their inertia, stay almost still because the friction acts for only a very short time.
**Coin on a card over a glass**: flick the card away and the coin drops into the glass instead of moving with the card.
Standing passengers on a bus **lurch backwards** when the bus suddenly accelerates: their bodies tend to stay at rest while the bus moves forward.
Shaking water off your hands: your hands stop, but the drops carry on moving.
A hammer head can be tightened by banging the handle down: the handle stops, the head keeps moving down onto it.

callouts.p: Use the structure: the object was at rest (or moving); because of its inertia it tends to stay that way; the force on it was too small or too brief to change its velocity much.

core.h: Inertial mass and weight are different
core.p: Mass and weight are often confused. Inertial mass is about resistance to acceleration; weight is a gravitational force.
bullets: **Inertial mass** (kg) is the same everywhere: on Earth, on the Moon and in deep space.
**Weight** (N) = mass x gravitational field strength, so it changes with location.
On the Moon (g about 1.6 N/kg) a 60 kg astronaut weighs about 96 N instead of about 600 N on Earth, but is just as hard to accelerate sideways.
In orbit an astronaut feels weightless, yet a heavy piece of equipment is still hard to start and stop moving.
Experiments show that the mass that resists acceleration and the mass that is pulled by gravity are equal, which is why all objects fall with the same acceleration (without air resistance).

callouts.p: An astronaut in orbit still has their full inertial mass, so a big force is still needed to change their velocity quickly.

core.p: Newton's first law is sometimes called the law of inertia. The two ideas describe the same behaviour.
bullets: First law: zero resultant force means no change in velocity.
Inertia: objects tend not to change their velocity.
Inertial mass: tells you **how much** they resist that change.
Second law: how big the change is: a = F / m.
Together: a large resultant force and a small inertial mass give the quickest change of velocity.

callouts.p: First law (no resultant, no change), inertia (tendency not to change), inertial mass (how strongly it resists), second law (how much change for a given force).

core.p: Inertial mass matters just as much for stopping as for starting.
bullets: For a given braking force, the deceleration is a = F / m, so a larger mass decelerates less.
A smaller deceleration means the vehicle takes **more time and more distance** to stop.
This is why lorries keep longer gaps and have lower speed limits on some roads.
Doubling the load roughly halves the deceleration for the same braking force.
Engineers fit larger brakes to heavier vehicles to give a larger braking force.

callouts.p: Write a = F / m and say that a larger m with the same F gives a smaller a: concise and worth the mark.

core.h: Changing direction needs a force too
core.p: Inertia resists any change in velocity, and velocity includes direction.
bullets: A car turning a corner needs a sideways (centripetal) resultant force from friction between tyres and road.
Passengers feel themselves 'thrown' outwards on a bend: in fact their bodies tend to continue in a straight line while the car turns.
On ice, friction is small, so the car tends to keep moving in a straight line and fails to turn.
A heavier vehicle needs a larger sideways force to turn the same corner at the same speed.
A hammer thrower lets go and the hammer flies off in a straight line at a tangent to the circle.

callouts.p: There is no force pushing passengers outwards on a bend. They are continuing in a straight line because of inertia.

core.p: Calculations use inertial mass = force / acceleration. Make sure the force is the **resultant** force.
bullets: Write: m = F / a.
Find the resultant force first if more than one force acts.
Find acceleration from (v - u) / t if needed.
Give the answer in kg.
Check: a heavy object should come out with a large inertial mass; a tiny acceleration for a big force means large mass.

callouts.p: N divided by m/s squared gives kg. If your answer is in some other unit, you have used the wrong quantities.

analogy.p: Inertia is like a trolley's stubbornness: once parked it does not want to move, and once rolling it does not want to stop or turn. Inertial mass is how stubborn it is: a trolley full of bottled water is far more stubborn than an empty one, and you measure that stubbornness by how hard you must push to get a certain speed-up. The analogy breaks down because stubbornness suggests the trolley chooses to resist, and suggests a resisting force; really inertia is a property of matter, not a force, and in space a trolley with no friction would keep rolling forever.

terms.d: The tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.
A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object; inertial mass = force / acceleration.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; the same everywhere.
The gravitational force on an object, W = m g, measured in newtons.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces on an object combined.
The rate of change of velocity, in m/s squared.
Speed in a stated direction.
With zero resultant force an object stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity.
Resultant force = mass x acceleration.
One quantity divided by another; inertial mass is the ratio of force to acceleration.
When one quantity doubles, the other halves; acceleration is inversely proportional to mass for a fixed force.
The force per unit mass due to gravity, about 10 N/kg on Earth and about 1.6 N/kg on the Moon.
A restraint that applies a backward force to decelerate a passenger with the car.
A decrease in velocity, caused by a resultant force opposite to the motion.

mistakes.w: Inertia is the force that keeps an object moving.
mistakes.r: Inertia is a property (tendency to keep its velocity), not a force; no force is needed to keep moving at constant velocity.

mistakes.w: When a car brakes, the passenger is thrown forward by a force.
mistakes.r: The passenger continues moving forward because of inertia while the car decelerates; the seat belt applies a backward force.

mistakes.w: Inertial mass = mass x acceleration.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass = force / acceleration.

mistakes.w: Astronauts in orbit have no mass because they are weightless.
mistakes.r: They still have the same inertial mass; only the apparent weight changes.

mistakes.w: Objects on the Moon are easier to accelerate sideways because they weigh less.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass is the same on the Moon, so the same force gives the same acceleration (ignoring friction).

mistakes.w: A heavier object has less inertia because gravity pulls it more.
mistakes.r: More mass means more inertia: it is harder to change its velocity.

mistakes.w: Inertial mass is measured in newtons.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass is measured in kilograms.

mistakes.w: On a bend, a force pushes passengers outwards.
mistakes.r: Their bodies tend to keep moving in a straight line because of inertia while the car turns.

exam.q: What is meant by inertia?
model: The tendency of an object to remain at rest or to continue moving at constant velocity (unless a resultant force acts)
exam.tip: Include both the 'at rest' and 'moving' cases.

exam.q: Define inertial mass.
model: A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object
defined as force / acceleration
exam.tip: Two parts: what it measures, and the ratio.

exam.q: A resultant force of 18 N gives an object an acceleration of 1.5 m/s squared. Calculate the inertial mass.
model: = 12 kg
exam.tip: Unit kg.

exam.q: Object A accelerates at 4 m/s squared and object B at 1 m/s squared when the same resultant force acts on each. Which has the larger inertial mass and by what factor?
model: B has the larger inertial mass
4 times larger (since m = F / a and a is 4 times smaller)
exam.tip: Same F, so mass is inversely proportional to a.

exam.q: Explain why a passenger without a seat belt can hit the windscreen when a car stops suddenly.
model: The braking force acts on the car, which decelerates
The passenger has inertia and continues moving forward at the original speed
No (or too small a) backward force acts on the passenger until they hit the windscreen
exam.tip: Avoid saying the passenger is thrown forward by a force.

exam.q: An astronaut on the Moon finds it easier to lift a rock than on Earth, but just as hard to push it to start it rolling along a smooth surface. Explain.
model: Lifting depends on weight; weight = m g
g on the Moon is smaller so the rock's weight is smaller
Starting it moving depends on inertial mass
Inertial mass is the same on the Moon, so the same force is needed for the same acceleration
exam.tip: Separate weight (gravity) from inertial mass (resistance to acceleration).

exam.q: A student plots a graph of resultant force (y-axis) against acceleration (x-axis) for a trolley. The line passes through the origin with a gradient of 0.8. What does the gradient represent and what is its value with unit?
model: The inertial mass of the trolley
0.8 kg
exam.tip: Gradient = rise / run = F / a.

exam.q: Describe how you could measure the inertial mass of a trolley in the laboratory.
model: Pull the trolley with a string over a pulley to hanging masses; force = weight of hanging masses (m g)
Use a card and two light gates (or a data logger) to measure speeds at two points
Calculate acceleration = change in speed / time
Repeat for a range of forces, repeating each and taking means
Compensate for friction (slightly tilt the runway) and keep the total mass being accelerated constant
Plot force against acceleration; the gradient of the line through the origin is the inertial mass
exam.tip: Link the method to the definition m = F / a.

exam.q: Explain why a fully loaded lorry needs a longer distance to stop than the same lorry when empty, for the same braking force.
model: The loaded lorry has a greater inertial mass
For the same force the deceleration is smaller (a = F / m)
So it takes longer and travels further before stopping
exam.tip: Use the equation in words.

exam.q: Explain the coin and card trick: a card is flicked quickly from under a coin resting on top of a glass, and the coin falls into the glass.
model: The coin is at rest and has inertia, so it tends to stay at rest
The friction force from the card acts for a very short time, so it hardly changes the coin's velocity
Once the card is gone, the only force is the coin's weight, so it falls into the glass
exam.tip: Mention why the small brief force produces little change in velocity.

worked.q: A sledge is pulled with a force of 60 N. Friction on it is 15 N. It accelerates at 1.5 m/s squared. Calculate the inertial mass of the sledge and rider.
steps: Resultant force = 60 - 15 = 45 N
Inertial mass = force / acceleration
m = 30 kg

worked.q: A 0.5 kg ball and a 4.0 kg medicine ball are each pushed with a resultant force of 8 N. Calculate each acceleration and compare.
steps: Ball: a = F / m = 8 / 0.5 = 16 m/s squared
Medicine ball: a = 8 / 4.0 = 2 m/s squared
The medicine ball has 8 times the inertial mass
So its acceleration is 8 times smaller: its velocity is harder to change
worked.ans: 16 m/s squared and 2 m/s squared; the medicine ball has 8 times the inertial mass.

worked.q: An astronaut of mass 70 kg is in deep space, far from any planet. A crewmate pushes her with a resultant force of 35 N. Calculate her acceleration and explain why her weightlessness does not make it larger.
steps: Inertial mass is 70 kg everywhere, including in deep space
a = 0.5 m/s squared
Weightlessness means no noticeable gravitational force, but inertial mass, which resists acceleration, is unchanged
worked.ans: 0.5 m/s squared, the same as it would be on a frictionless surface on Earth.

phy_ocra.4.5.summary: **Momentum** is a property of every moving object, defined as **momentum = mass x velocity (p = m v)**, measured in **kg m/s**. Because velocity is a vector, momentum is a vector too, so its direction matters. In a **closed system** (no external forces) the **total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it**: this is **conservation of momentum**. It lets you predict the velocities of objects after collisions and explosions, such as cars crashing, snooker balls, and a gun recoiling.

core.p: Momentum describes how much 'motion' an object has. It depends on both how much mass is moving and how fast and in which direction it moves.
bullets: **Momentum = mass x velocity**, p = m v.
A heavy lorry and a light car at the same speed: the lorry has more momentum.
A bullet has a small mass but a very large velocity, so it can have a large momentum.
An object at rest has **zero momentum**.
The larger the momentum, the larger the force or the longer the time needed to stop the object.

callouts.p: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity: momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) x velocity (m/s).
p = m v. You need to recall this; it is not on the equation sheet.

core.p: Using SI units makes momentum come out in kg m/s.
bullets: Mass m in **kilograms (kg)**.
Velocity v in **metres per second (m/s)**.
Momentum p in **kilogram metres per second (kg m/s)**.
To find velocity: **v = p / m**. To find mass: **m = p / v**.
Convert grams to kg and km/h to m/s first (divide km/h by 3.6).

callouts.p: Momentum is not measured in newtons or in m/s. Write kg m/s.

core.p: Velocity has a direction, so momentum does too. Two objects can have the same size of momentum but in opposite directions.
bullets: Choose one direction as **positive** (usually to the right).
Velocities, and so momenta, in the opposite direction are **negative**.
A 2 kg ball at 3 m/s to the right has p = +6 kg m/s; at 3 m/s to the left, p = -6 kg m/s.
Two equal and opposite momenta add up to **zero total momentum**.
Getting the signs right is the key to collision and explosion questions.

callouts.p: Write 'taking right as positive' at the start of your working. It shows the examiner you are handling direction.

core.p: When objects interact, they push on each other with equal and opposite forces for the same time, so the momentum one gains is exactly the momentum the other loses.
bullets: In a **closed system**, the **total momentum before = total momentum after** a collision or explosion.
A closed system is one where **no external forces** act (or they are balanced), so nothing from outside adds or removes momentum.
Momentum can be transferred from one object to another, but the total stays the same.
This applies to collisions where objects bounce off, collisions where they stick together, and explosions.
Real situations are only approximately closed: friction and air resistance are external forces that slowly reduce the total.

callouts.p: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.
Newton's third law: during the collision the forces on the two objects are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so the changes in momentum are equal and opposite.

core.p: If two objects join after a collision, they move off with one shared velocity. Use the combined mass after the collision.
bullets: Total momentum before = m1 u1 + m2 u2.
Total momentum after = (m1 + m2) v.
Set them equal and solve for the unknown.
Example: a 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick: 2 x 3 + 1 x 0 = 3 x v, so v = 2 m/s.
The joined objects always move **more slowly** than the moving object did before, because the same momentum is shared by more mass.

callouts.p: After sticking, add the masses before multiplying by the shared velocity.

core.p: If the objects separate after the collision, each has its own velocity afterwards.
bullets: Total momentum before = m1 u1 + m2 u2.
Total momentum after = m1 v1 + m2 v2.
You will be given all but one value; solve for the unknown.
A velocity that comes out negative means that object moves in the **negative direction** (it has bounced back).
Snooker: a moving cue ball hits a stationary ball head-on; the cue ball nearly stops and the target ball moves off with almost the same velocity, because the balls have equal mass.

callouts.t: Momentum conserved, kinetic energy usually not
callouts.p: Total momentum is conserved in every collision in a closed system, but some kinetic energy is usually transferred to heating and sound, so the kinetic energy after is often less.

core.p: In an explosion the objects start at rest, so the **total momentum before is zero**. It must still be zero afterwards.
bullets: After an explosion the pieces move in **opposite directions** with equal-sized but opposite momenta.
m1 v1 + m2 v2 = 0, so m1 v1 = -m2 v2.
The **lighter** piece moves off **faster**; the heavier piece moves more slowly.
**Gun recoil**: the bullet gains forward momentum, so the gun gains equal backward momentum and recoils.
Other examples: a cannon recoiling, a person jumping off a boat (the boat moves back), two skaters pushing apart, a spring pushing two trolleys apart.
Rockets: exhaust gases are pushed backwards with momentum, so the rocket gains equal forward momentum.

callouts.p: Starting from rest, total momentum = 0 before and after. The momenta of the pieces must cancel out.

core.p: Follow the same steps every time and collision questions become routine.
bullets: 1. Draw a quick before-and-after sketch with masses and velocities.
2. State a positive direction.
3. Work out the total momentum before (add each m v with signs).
4. Write an expression for the total momentum after, including the unknown.
5. Set before = after and solve.
6. Give the answer with unit and direction, and check it is sensible.

callouts.p: Write 'momentum before = momentum after' as a line of working. It often earns the first mark even if later arithmetic goes wrong.

core.p: A momentum bar chart shows how the total is shared out before and after a collision while the total itself stays fixed.
bullets: Before the sticking collision only trolley A is moving: all 6 kg m/s belongs to A.
After the collision A has 2 x 2 = 4 kg m/s and B has 1 x 2 = 2 kg m/s.
The bars are different heights for each object, but the **totals are equal**.
Momentum lost by one object = momentum gained by the other.
The same picture with a zero total describes an explosion.

callouts.p: Momentum is transferred between objects in a collision; it is never created or destroyed in a closed system.

core.p: Conservation of momentum can be tested with trolleys on a runway, using light gates to measure velocities.
bullets: Fix a card to each trolley and place a light gate before and after the collision point.
Measure the velocity of trolley A before the collision (card length / time).
Use Velcro or a pin and cork so the trolleys stick, or springs so they bounce apart.
Measure the velocity (or velocities) after the collision.
Measure the masses with a balance; calculate total momentum before and after.
Tilt the runway slightly to compensate for friction so the system is closer to closed; the totals should be equal within experimental error.

callouts.t: Why the totals may differ slightly
callouts.p: Friction and air resistance are external forces, and timing and mass measurements have uncertainty. Expect totals to be close, not identical.

core.p: Stopping a moving object means reducing its momentum to zero. How quickly that happens decides how large the force is (the detailed rate-of-change link is a separate point).
bullets: A larger momentum needs a larger force or a longer time to bring it to rest.
Crumple zones, seat belts, airbags, crash helmets, and cushioned playground surfaces all **increase the time** over which momentum changes, which **reduces the force**.
Heavier and faster vehicles have more momentum, so crashes involving them are more dangerous.
Catching a ball: moving your hands back with the ball increases the stopping time and reduces the sting.
In a collision between a car and a lorry, both experience the same size force, but the car (smaller mass) has a much bigger change in velocity.

callouts.p: Safety features do not absorb momentum; they increase the time taken for the momentum to change, so the force is smaller.

analogy.p: Think of momentum as money in a closed room of people. When two people collide, one hands some money to the other: one loses exactly what the other gains, so the total in the room never changes. Money in one pocket going 'left' counts as negative, so two people with equal and opposite amounts have a total of zero, like an explosion from rest. The analogy breaks down because momentum depends on both mass and velocity and is a vector with direction, whereas money is a single positive amount; and real rooms are not perfectly closed, just as friction lets momentum leak out to the Earth.

terms.d: The product of mass and velocity, p = m v, measured in kg m/s.
Speed in a given direction; a vector quantity.
A quantity with both size and direction, such as momentum, velocity and force.
A quantity with size only, such as mass and speed.
In a closed system the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it.
A system on which no external resultant force acts, so total momentum stays constant.
A force on the system from something outside it, such as friction from the ground.
An event in which two or more objects exert forces on each other for a short time.
An event in which objects initially at rest (or together) are pushed apart.
The backward movement of an object, such as a gun, when it pushes another object forwards.
The total mass of objects that move together after sticking.
Choosing one direction as positive and the opposite as negative.
The unit of momentum: kilogram metres per second.
A sensor that times how long a card blocks a light beam so speed can be calculated.
Part of a car designed to deform in a crash, increasing the collision time and reducing the force.

mistakes.w: Momentum = mass x speed, and direction does not matter.
mistakes.r: Momentum = mass x velocity; it is a vector so direction must be included with a sign.

mistakes.w: Momentum is measured in N or kg/m/s.
mistakes.r: Momentum is measured in kg m/s.

mistakes.w: After an explosion from rest, total momentum is the sum of the sizes of the two momenta.
mistakes.r: The momenta are in opposite directions; the total is zero.

mistakes.w: When two trolleys stick, using only one trolley's mass after the collision.
mistakes.r: Use the combined mass (m1 + m2) after the collision.

mistakes.w: Momentum is conserved in all situations.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved in a closed system, where no external forces act.

mistakes.w: Kinetic energy and momentum are both always conserved in collisions.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved in a closed system; kinetic energy is often partly transferred to heating and sound.

mistakes.w: The gun recoils because the bullet pushes air back onto it.
mistakes.r: The bullet gains forward momentum so the gun gains equal backward momentum (total stays zero).

mistakes.w: Airbags absorb the momentum of the passenger.
mistakes.r: Airbags increase the time taken for the passenger's momentum to reach zero, reducing the force.

exam.q: Write down the equation linking momentum, mass and velocity.
model: momentum = mass x velocity (p = m v)
exam.tip: Velocity, not speed.

exam.q: Calculate the momentum of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s.
exam.tip: Include the unit kg m/s.

exam.q: A ball of mass 0.16 kg has a momentum of 4.8 kg m/s. Calculate its velocity.
exam.tip: Rearrange first.

exam.q: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
model: In a closed system (no external forces)
total momentum before an event = total momentum after
exam.tip: The 'closed system' condition is often the second mark.

exam.q: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision.
model: Momentum before = 3 x 4 + 1 x 0 = 12 kg m/s
Momentum after = (3 + 1) x v
exam.tip: Use the combined mass after.

exam.q: A rifle of mass 4.0 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.010 kg at 400 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
model: Total momentum before = 0
Momentum of bullet = 0.010 x 400 = 4.0 kg m/s
Rifle velocity = -4.0 / 4.0 = 1.0 m/s backwards (opposite to bullet)
exam.tip: Give the direction of the recoil.

exam.q: Explain why a gun recoils when it is fired.
model: Before firing, total momentum is zero
The bullet gains momentum forwards
Momentum is conserved so the gun must gain equal momentum backwards
exam.tip: Use 'momentum is conserved'.

exam.q: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 6 m/s to the right hits a 1.5 kg ball at rest. After the collision the 0.5 kg ball moves at 3 m/s to the left. Calculate the velocity of the 1.5 kg ball.
model: Taking right as positive, momentum before = 0.5 x 6 = 3 kg m/s
Momentum after = 0.5 x (-3) + 1.5 v
v = 3 m/s to the right
exam.tip: The bounce-back velocity is negative.

exam.q: Describe how you could use trolleys and light gates to show that momentum is conserved in a collision.
model: Measure masses of both trolleys with a balance
Attach cards; measure the velocity of trolley A before collision with a light gate (card length / time)
Trolley B at rest; trolleys collide and stick (Velcro or pin and cork)
Measure the velocity after the collision with a second light gate
Calculate total momentum before (mA uA) and after ((mA + mB) v)
Compensate for friction by tilting the runway; repeat; show totals are equal within experimental error
exam.tip: Say what is measured, how, and how momentum is calculated.

exam.q: Two ice skaters stand at rest together and push apart. Skater A (50 kg) moves off at 2.4 m/s. Skater B moves off at 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction. Calculate the mass of skater B.
model: Total momentum before = 0, so momenta after are equal and opposite
exam.tip: Sizes of the two momenta are equal.

exam.q: Explain why momentum is not quite conserved when two trolleys collide on a rough bench.
model: Friction is an external force acting on the trolleys
so the system is not closed and some momentum is lost (transferred to the Earth)
exam.tip: Name the external force.

worked.q: A 1200 kg car moving at 15 m/s crashes into the back of a stationary 800 kg car. They lock together. Calculate the speed of the wreckage just after the collision.
steps: Momentum before = 1200 x 15 + 800 x 0 = 18 000 kg m/s
Combined mass = 1200 + 800 = 2000 kg
Momentum after = 2000 x v
worked.ans: 9 m/s in the original direction of the moving car

worked.q: A 60 kg person steps forward off a 120 kg boat at rest, moving at 2.0 m/s. Ignoring water resistance, calculate the velocity of the boat.
steps: Total momentum before = 0
Momentum of person = 60 x 2.0 = 120 kg m/s forwards
Boat must have 120 kg m/s backwards
v = 120 / 120 = 1.0 m/s backwards
worked.ans: 1.0 m/s in the opposite direction to the person

worked.q: Two trolleys head towards each other. Trolley A (2.0 kg) moves right at 3.0 m/s; trolley B (1.0 kg) moves left at 2.0 m/s. They stick together. Find the velocity afterwards.
steps: Take right as positive
Momentum before = 2.0 x 3.0 + 1.0 x (-2.0) = 6.0 - 2.0 = 4.0 kg m/s
Combined mass = 3.0 kg
v = 4.0 / 3.0 = 1.3 m/s (to 2 s.f.), positive so to the right
